description: Basal cell carcinoma is the most common type of skin cancer, arising from basal keratinocytes in the top layer of the skin. It is a common, locally invasive, keratinocyte cancer that typically grows slowly and rarely spreads (metastasizes) to other parts of the body, but it can invade and destroy surrounding tissue if left untreated. It most commonly develops on sun-exposed skin such as the face.
symptoms: A firm, round, raised growth, often shiny and pink/red on lighter skin tones or brown/black on darker skin tones
A sore that does not heal, or heals and returns
A new mark on the skin that looks like a scar
"Rodent ulcer" appearance - raised, pearly edges with central atrophy or ulceration, and prominent capillary networks
Slowly growing plaque or nodule, skin-colored, pink, or pigmented, ranging from a few millimeters to several centimeters
Superficial form: a scaly, red, flat mark, possibly crusty, rough, or itchy
Most are painless, though some can be itchy or bleed
Approximately 80% occur on the face and neck, but can also occur on hands, forearms, back, and lower legs
warning_signs: Bleeding, crusting over, and breaking open repeatedly as the growth enlarges
Growth that is enlarging, or has changed color or texture
A growth or area of skin that hurts, itches, bleeds, crusts, or scabs for more than 4 weeks
Irritation from rubbing, catching on clothing/jewelry, or injury, with pain, itching, numbness, or extreme sensitivity
Rare but noted: a small proportion of BCCs grow rapidly, invade deeply, and/or metastasize to local lymph nodes (aggressive subtypes)
recommendation: See a dermatologist if a lesion is growing, bleeding, not healing, or changing in any way. Diagnosis is usually confirmed pathologically via biopsy or excision. Regular self-skin exams and annual professional skin checks are recommended, since about half of people with one BCC develop a second within 3 years.
